qrdBas-c50824-d1e101.summary: Rubric introducing the single question on distinction 24 of Book 3.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e108.summary: Notes that the traditional question on this distinction, whether faith and science can coexist about the same object in the same intellect, was adequately treated in the first question of Book 1, and so substitutes another question: whether God is the per se first object of faith under the proper ratio of deity.
claims: The compossibility of faith and science was settled in the first question of Book 1.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e132.summary: First argument for the negative: two repugnant and incompossible habits cannot have the same object under the same ratio; but faith and evident science of God, whether of wayfarers or of the blessed, are repugnant and cannot coexist.
claims: Incompossible habits cannot share an object under the same ratio.
Faith and evident knowledge of God are incompossible.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e143.summary: Second argument for the negative: two virtues differing in species and genus and belonging to different powers cannot have the same object under the same ratio; but God under the proper ratio of deity is the object of charity, which belongs to the will, so not of faith, which belongs to the intellect.
claims: Virtues of different powers have different formal objects.
God under the ratio of deity is the object of charity.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e160.summary: Third argument for the negative: the object of the intellect is the true and its formal ratio is truth; since faith belongs to the intellect, God, even if the per se first object of faith, is so under the ratio of truth rather than of deity. The paragraph ends with the opening words of the following contrary argument, displaced in the witness.
claims: The formal ratio of the intellect's object is truth.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e178.summary: Argument to the contrary: faith and the doctrine of faith have the same object under the same ratio; the object of the doctrine of faith, our theology, is God under the proper ratio of deity, as shown in Book 1. The paragraph closes by introducing the plan of the question.
claims: Faith and theology share the same object under the same ratio.
The subject of our theology is God under the ratio of deity.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e191.summary: First point of the plan: to inquire into the per se first object of faith and its ratio, and into the secondary objects.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e198.summary: Second point of the plan: whether it is meritorious to believe by faith in objects exceeding the capacity of nature. (In the body this becomes the third article, after an unannounced article on the unity of the habit of faith.)

qrdBas-c50824-d1e205.summary: Final point of the plan: replies to the opening arguments.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e210.summary: Opens the first article with a common presupposition: God is the primary and per se object of faith, because faith is a theological virtue regarding God as its immediate first object and end, because God is the subject of the articles of faith, and because everything else falls under faith by attribution to God.
claims: God is the primary per se object of faith.
As a theological virtue faith regards God as immediate object and end.
God is the subject of the articles of faith.
Other things fall under faith by attribution to God.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e231.summary: Presents the first opinion on the formal ratio of faith's object: God is its per se first object under the ratio of 'the revealed' (ratio revelati), so that nothing is believed or assented to by faith except insofar as revealed. It is supported because there is no faith about what is unrevealed or naturally attainable (even about God), because faith rests especially on revealed Scripture and the sayings of saints to whom God revealed, and because faith concerns what does not appear and cannot be known unless revealed. The paragraph ends with the opening words of the next opinion, displaced in the witness.
claims: According to this opinion, being revealed is the formal objective ratio of faith.
There is no faith about what is naturally knowable.
Faith rests on revealed Scripture and the saints.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e260.summary: Presents the second opinion: God is the object of faith under the ratio of the non-apparent, so that non-appearance, non-evidence, or obscurity is the formal ratio in faith's object. It is supported by Hebrews 11 ('faith is the argument of things not appearing') and Augustine ('faith is to believe what you do not see'), because this distinguishes faith from science and any clear cognition of an evident object, and because faith and hope tend to the same thing, and hope tends to the unseen. The paragraph ends with words introducing a possible third opinion, displaced in the witness.
claims: According to this opinion, non-appearance or obscurity is the formal ratio of faith's object.
Non-evidence distinguishes faith from science.
Faith and hope share an unseen object.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e291.summary: Adds and dismisses a third opinion: God is the object of faith under the ratio of the credible, as something is the object of sight under the ratio of the visible, since faith is a believing habit and the knowable as such is the object of science. Bassolis rejects this: 'credible' names only a denomination of reason and a relation in the object, while faith is a real habit; likewise for the knowable and the visible, whose real objects are something real by its own ratio, such as color or light. The paragraph ends with words introducing the refutation of the first opinion.
claims: The ratio of the credible is only a rational denomination and relation.
A real habit requires a real formal object.
The object of science or sight is something real, not the knowable or visible as such.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e317.summary: First argument against the first opinion: a real habit, as distinct from a habit of reason, must have a real formal objective ratio, since it is measured by its object; faith is such a habit, but being revealed in the object implies only a relation of reason.
claims: A real habit is measured by and requires a real formal object.
Being revealed is only a relation of reason in the object.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e341.summary: Second argument against the first opinion, attributed to others: if being revealed is faith's formal ratio, nothing, including God or the article that God is triune and one, is believed except insofar as revealed. But then one must know that it is revealed, which can only be by faith, so one must believe that it is revealed, and believe that only because that too is revealed, and so on to infinity.
claims: If revealedness were the formal ratio of faith, believing anything would require believing it revealed.
This generates an infinite regress of beliefs about revelation.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e370.summary: Third argument against the first opinion: the object of vision is not God as seen, since 'being seen' in God implies only a relation of reason to the seer; likewise the object of faith is not God as revealed, nor even, a fortiori, God as believed. The paragraph ends with words introducing the refutation of the second opinion.
claims: Being seen posits only a relation of reason in God.
Faith's object is neither God as revealed nor God as believed.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e387.summary: First argument against the second opinion: the per se first object of a positive and real habit can only be posited under a positive formal ratio, but non-appearance or non-seeing is negative.
claims: A positive real habit requires a positive formal ratio in its object.
Non-appearance is a negative ratio.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e398.summary: Second argument against the second opinion: if God under the ratio of non-appearance were faith's formal object, by parity God under the ratio of appearance or being seen would be the formal object of evident cognition or vision; but this is false, since such a ratio either says nothing on God's side or only a relation of reason, which cannot beatify.
claims: By parity, the opinion would make 'being seen' the formal object of vision.
A relation of reason cannot beatify.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e414.summary: Third argument against the second opinion: a habit must be reducible to its object according to the object's formal ratio, but affirmation is not reduced to negation nor the positive to the negative. The paragraph ends with words introducing Bassolis's own position on the article.
claims: A positive habit cannot be reduced to a negative formal ratio.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e425.summary: Bassolis's first conclusion: the per se first object of faith is something incomplex, namely God, under the formal ratio of proper deity and not any other ratio, just as the per se first object of the science of faith, our theology, is God under the ratio of deity, as shown in Book 1; nearly the same arguments prove this for faith.
claims: The per se first object of faith is incomplex: God.
God is faith's object under the formal ratio of deity, not of revealedness, non-appearance, or credibility.
Faith and theology share the same first object under the same ratio.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e445.summary: Second conclusion: other things are secondary objects of faith reduced to the first, especially complex objects such as the articles of faith formed about God as primary object, just as scientific conclusions predicating attributes of a subject are complex objects of science. The articles, as complex propositions, are what is assented to in believing, since assent properly regards a complex truth rather than a simple term. Belief in these complex truths most evidently distinguishes the believer from the unbeliever: many unbelievers believe that God exists but not the articles formed about him, and do not properly believe in God, as in the Master's distinction 24 on believing God, believing that there is a God, and believing in God. The paragraph ends with words introducing the replies to the opinions.
claims: The articles of faith are complex secondary objects of faith reduced to God as primary object.
Assent properly bears on complex truths rather than simple terms.
Belief in the articles, not mere belief that God exists, distinguishes believer from unbeliever.
Unbelievers who believe God exists do not properly believe in God.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e493.summary: Reply to the arguments for the first opinion: even granting that faith is about revealed things (and perhaps also demonstrated ones) and rests on revealed Scripture and the saints, especially acquired faith, which rests on the testimony of others and on miracles that reasonably move one to believe by right reason (infused faith rests immediately on God alone), it does not follow that revealedness is the formal objective ratio. Neither are 'believed', 'written', or 'testified', just as 'known' is not the formal objective ratio of science although science is of the known.
claims: That faith concerns revealed things does not make revealedness its formal object.
Acquired faith rests on testimony and miracles; infused faith rests immediately on God alone.
Faith may extend to demonstrated as well as revealed truths.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e533.summary: Reply to the first argument of the second opinion: faith is of non-appearing things because it is not of itself evident cognition and its object is not evident through faith, though it may be evident from elsewhere (as said in Book 1). Yet non-evidence is not the formal objective ratio; perhaps it is not a ratio on the object's side at all, but a negative extrinsic denomination from the act or habit of faith, which is not clear about the object. Even if it were on the object's side, it could not be the formal ratio, as shown.
claims: Faith is not of itself evident, though its object may be evident from another source.
Non-evidence is an extrinsic negative denomination from the act of faith, not a formal ratio of the object.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e564.summary: Reply to the second argument of the second opinion: faith is not primarily distinguished from science or evident knowledge of God by having non-appearance as its formal ratio, but because the cognition of faith is of itself enigmatic and inevident while science or vision is evident, even about the same object under the same formal ratio.
claims: Faith and science differ by the mode of cognition, enigmatic versus evident, not by formal object.
Faith and science can share the same object under the same formal ratio.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e582.summary: Reply to the third argument of the second opinion: though hope, like faith, tends to the unseen, the ratio of the unseen is not the formal ratio of its object, but rather the ratio of deity.
claims: The formal ratio of hope's object, as of faith's, is deity, not unseenness.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e589.summary: Opens the second article on infused faith: it is one numerically identical habit in its possessor with respect to all credibles, whether the first incomplex credible, God, or the complex credibles, the articles and what can be deduced from them. There is no need to posit many habits, as there is no need to posit many infused habits of charity for the many things loved from charity. The reason is that neither infused charity nor infused faith is generated by diverse acts about diverse objects, and each regards one simple first object as per se primary, so neither is multiplied or varied according to acts of different kinds about different objects.
claims: Infused faith is numerically one habit regarding all credibles.
Infused habits are not generated by acts and so are not multiplied by diverse acts.
Infused faith, like charity, regards one simple first object.
concepts: unity of the habit of faith

qrdBas-c50824-d1e631.summary: On acquired faith, which is more doubtful: it is not one habit but many, one concerning God as per se primary object (unique in its possessor, as infused faith is in its way) and others concerning each article singly. They are many because generated by many acts of different kinds about objects (the articles) of different kinds that are the primary objects of those habits; one can be acquired, possessed, or corrupted without another, as experience of repeated acts about different articles shows. So acquired faith deals with God by a first habit and with complex objects by other habits and acts, as said in Book 1 about the unity of our theology. Thus a heretic can err about one article while firmly holding all the others by acquired faith. Paul's 'one faith' is true of infused faith in each person, or of faith in general, as of baptism in general.
claims: Acquired faith is a plurality of habits, one for God and one for each article.
Acquired habits are individuated by the acts and objects that generate them.
One acquired habit of faith can exist or be lost without the others.
A heretic can err in one article while holding the others with acquired faith.
'One faith' (Ephesians 4) refers to infused faith or faith in general.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e712.summary: Opens the third article with objections to the claim that believing all the objects of faith is meritorious or reasonable: the believer exposes himself to danger by believing what he cannot know to be true; he believes without reason and rejects natural reason ('faith has no merit where human reason provides proof'); either he has a necessary motive, in which case he would believe necessarily, or a probable one, in which case he should believe only probably, not firmly; and the chief reasonable motive, the multitude of miracles for the Christian faith, is unreliable since miracles deceive, as those of Antichrist will. The paragraph ends with words introducing Bassolis's reply.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e755.summary: Against these, it is reasonable and can be meritorious to believe what the faithful and the Church hold, all the articles and their deductions, despite their inevidence. Motives of credibility: these truths are approved by a great and concordant multitude of proven men who condemned lying in Scripture and are unlikely to be liars; those who spread them were poor, humble, and unlettered, yet subjugated the whole world, itself a great miracle; they commonly despised this life and gave their lives to confirm them; and they confirmed the faith by frequent, unusual, unheard-of miracles.
claims: Believing the articles of faith is reasonable and can be meritorious despite inevidence.
The concordant testimony of many trustworthy witnesses supports the faith.
The spread of the faith by humble men is itself a miracle.
Martyrdom and miracles confirm the faith.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e792.summary: Deferring the objection that these miracles may be deceptive like Antichrist's, Bassolis concludes that it is reasonable even by natural reason to believe what faith holds. A person arising now in purely natural condition, presented with a faith held from antiquity by so great a company of people free from worldly sins against right reason and approved by so many unusual signs, would judge by right natural reason that it should be held. So it is reasonable to believe everything belonging to faith and deducible from it, and such an act is meritorious de condigno if formed by charity and duly circumstanced. The paragraph ends with words introducing the replies.
claims: Believing the faith is reasonable by natural reason alone.
A person in pure naturals would judge by right reason that the Christian faith should be held.
An act of faith formed by charity and duly circumstanced merits de condigno.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e831.summary: Reply to the first objection: the believer does not expose himself to danger by believing what he cannot evidently know to be true; otherwise anyone believing a deed they had not seen on the testimony of others, however upright, would endanger themselves, which is false. Rather the unbeliever exposes himself to danger and acts against right reason by disbelieving what is so approved.
claims: Believing on reliable testimony without evidence is not reckless.
Disbelieving well-approved testimony is against right reason.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e849.summary: Reply to the second objection: the believer believes without a reason producing evidence, since such a reason is not required for believing, but does not reject it as incompossible with faith; such a reason is compossible with faith in some articles, though one does not believe on its account, since one would believe nonetheless without it. Yet one does not believe irrationally; believing is rather reasonable, as said.
claims: Faith does not require an evidence-producing reason.
Evident reasons are compossible with faith about the same articles.
Faith is not irrational but reasonable.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e873.summary: Reply to the third objection: the believer has no necessary middle term producing evidence about what is believed, nor requires one, but has a medium sufficiently inductive to belief by the judgment of right reason, so that he believes with certainty, not as an evident truth or on his own witness, but on sufficiently approved testimony of others, as people reasonably believe that Rome exists without ever having seen it.
claims: Faith lacks a necessary evidential medium.
Faith has a sufficient medium for certain belief: well-approved testimony.
Certainty can rest on others' testimony, as with belief in Rome's existence.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e895.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: the miracles performed in witness to the faith are a great motive for belief; Christ himself directed the Jews, who had believed Moses because of his miracles, to his works ('if you will not believe me, believe the works'). To the claim that miracles are deceptive, since Antichrist will work them, Bassolis replies that Christ, working true miracles, taught that Antichrist's would be false and not to be believed, and that some miracles under the law and faith Antichrist will never perform, such as the vision of the divine essence in Paul's rapture and revelations of future contingents found true in Scripture. Paul was neither lying, given his hatred of lies, nor deceived, since one can no more be deceived about a vision of the divine essence than about understanding a first principle.
claims: Miracles are a strong motive for faith, as Christ himself taught.
Christ's true miracles authenticate his warning that Antichrist's miracles will be false.
Some miracles, such as Paul's vision of God and true prophecy of future contingents, cannot be counterfeited by Antichrist.
One cannot be deceived about a vision of the divine essence any more than about a first principle.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e948.summary: Concludes: since God, who cannot be a false witness, worked these miracles in attestation of the faith and denounced others as false, the faith they support is to be believed. Many considerations can reasonably be brought against unbelievers: the authority of the writers and transmitters, the diligence of the recipients, the concord of the Scriptures, the reasonableness of the Christian law's content, the unreasonableness of contrary errors, the Church's stability in a law opposed to flesh and blood and to human inclinations, and the variety of miracles. Yet there is no certain demonstration, neither propter quid nor quia, that Christ was true God or even true man, even given his deeds, since all could have happened apparently or by a divine power assisting rather than united to a true man.
claims: God, who cannot witness falsely, attests the faith through miracles.
There are many reasonable arguments for the faith against unbelievers.
There is no demonstration, propter quid or quia, that Christ was true God or true man.
Christ's deeds are compatible with divine assistance without hypostatic union.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e1031.summary: Reply to the first opening argument: faith and any evident cognition of God, even that of the homeland, are not formally incompossible habits, as will appear later. Alternatively, even if they were, they could have the same object, as science and error, or contrary opinions, which are no less incompossible by nature, can be about the same object in the intellect.
claims: Faith and evident knowledge of God, even beatific, are not formally incompossible.
Even incompossible habits can have the same object.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e1016.summary: Reply to the second opening argument: its major premise is false, since faith and charity, though different habits in species and genus, can and do have the same object under the same formal ratio, God under the proper ratio of deity; indeed intellect and will have entirely the same formal object.
claims: Faith and charity share the same formal object, God under the ratio of deity.
Intellect and will have the same formal object.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e1034.summary: Reply to the third opening argument: Bassolis does not accept that the formal object of the intellect is being under the ratio of truth as distinguished from entity, as said elsewhere, since truth as such implies only a relation of reason to the intellect or the negation of difformity from it.
claims: The intellect's formal object is not being under the ratio of truth as distinct from being.
Truth as such is a relation of reason or a negation of difformity.

qrdBas-c50824-d1e1047.summary: Adds a note, following others: truth, goodness, and deity are entirely the same outside the intellect, so if one is the objective ratio of a habit or power, so is the other; hence intellect and will must have the same formal object, otherwise the willed would be understood only accidentally, through an annexed ratio, and conversely, which is false.
claims: Truth, goodness, and deity are really identical in God.
Intellect and will must therefore share the same formal object.

qrdBas-c50824-Dd1e215.summary: Article 1 asks under what formal ratio God is the per se first object of faith, granting the common view that God is that object. It presents three opinions: under the ratio of the revealed, under the ratio of the non-apparent (Hebrews 11, Augustine), and under the ratio of the credible. Bassolis dismisses the third as positing a mere denomination of reason, and refutes the first two: a real, positive habit requires a real, positive formal ratio, whereas revealedness is a relation of reason (and leads to an infinite regress of beliefs about revelation) and non-appearance is negative and, by parity, would make 'being seen' beatifying. He concludes that faith's first object is incomplex, God under the proper ratio of deity, as for theology, while the articles are complex secondary objects, assented to as propositions, which distinguish the believer from those who merely believe God exists. Faith's relation to revelation, testimony, and miracles does not make these its formal ratio; non-evidence is an extrinsic denomination from faith's enigmatic mode, which, not the object, distinguishes faith from science; hope, too, has deity as its formal ratio.
claims: God is the per se first object of faith under the formal ratio of deity.
Neither revealedness, non-appearance, nor credibility is the formal objective ratio of faith.
A real positive habit requires a real positive formal object.
The articles of faith are complex secondary objects reduced to God.
Faith and science differ in mode (enigmatic vs. evident), not in object.
Acquired faith rests on testimony and miracles; infused faith immediately on God.

qrdBas-c50824-Dd1e602.summary: Article 2, not announced in the plan, asks whether faith is one habit for all its objects. Infused faith is numerically one habit for God and all the articles and their deductions, just as one charity suffices for all things loved, since infused habits are not generated by acts and regard one simple first object. Acquired faith, by contrast, is many habits: one about God and one for each article, since generated by acts of different kinds about objects of different kinds, and separable from one another, as shown by experience and by the heretic who errs in one article while holding the others. Paul's 'one faith' refers to infused faith or faith in general.
claims: Infused faith is one numerical habit for all credibles.
Acquired faith is a plurality of habits, one for God and one for each article.
Acquired habits are individuated by the acts generating them.
A heretic can lose acquired faith in one article and retain it in others.
concepts: unity of the habit of faith

qrdBas-c50824-Dd1e733.summary: Article 3 asks whether believing objects that exceed natural capacity is reasonable and meritorious. Against objections that belief is reckless, irrational, either necessary or merely probable, and resting on deceptive miracles, Bassolis argues that believing the articles is reasonable even by natural reason, on account of the concordant testimony of trustworthy witnesses, the miraculous spread of the faith by humble men, martyrdom, and miracles; a person in pure naturals would judge the faith worth holding, and the act of faith formed by charity merits de condigno. Belief on approved testimony is not reckless (as believing in Rome unseen), needs no evidential reason though compossible with one, and gives certitude without evidence. Christ's true miracles authenticate his warning against Antichrist's, and some miracles, like Paul's vision of the divine essence and true prophecy, cannot be counterfeited. Many arguments support the faith against unbelievers, but there is no demonstration, quia or propter quid, that Christ was true God or true man.
claims: Believing the articles of faith is reasonable by natural reason and meritorious when formed by charity.
Faith rests on sufficiently approved testimony, giving certitude without evidence.
Christ's true miracles authenticate the faith and expose Antichrist's.
Some miracles, such as the vision of the divine essence, cannot be counterfeited.
There is no demonstration that Christ was true God or true man.

qrdBas-c50824-Dd1e1027.summary: Replies to the opening arguments. Faith and evident, even beatific, knowledge of God are not formally incompossible, and even incompossible habits can share an object. Faith and charity, though different habits, share the same formal object, God under the ratio of deity, and indeed intellect and will have the same formal object. The intellect's formal object is not being under the ratio of truth, since truth as such is only a relation of reason or a negation of difformity; and since truth, goodness, and deity are really identical outside the intellect, intellect and will must share a formal object.
claims: Faith and evident knowledge of God are compossible.
Faith and charity share the formal object of deity.
Intellect and will have the same formal object.
Truth as such is not the intellect's formal object.

qrdBas-c50824.summary: The single question on Book 3, distinction 24 sets aside the traditional question of whether faith and science can coexist about the same object (already settled in Book 1) and asks instead whether God is the per se first object of faith under the proper ratio of deity. Against arguments that faith and evident knowledge are incompossible, that deity is the object of charity rather than faith, and that the intellect's object is truth, and with the contrary argument that faith shares theology's object, Bassolis answers in three articles. First, he rejects the views that faith's formal ratio is revealedness, non-appearance, or credibility, since each is a relation of reason or a negation unfit to specify a real, positive habit, and holds that God under the ratio of deity is faith's incomplex first object, with the articles as complex secondary objects; faith differs from science by its enigmatic mode, not its object. Second, in an article not in his plan, he argues that infused faith is one habit for all credibles while acquired faith is many habits, one per article, which explains how a heretic can err in one article and hold the rest. Third, he defends the reasonableness and merit of believing what exceeds nature on the basis of testimony, the spread of the faith, martyrdom, and miracles that Antichrist cannot counterfeit, while denying that Christ's divinity or humanity can be demonstrated. The replies affirm that faith and evident knowledge are compossible and that intellect and will share the same formal object.
claims: God under the proper ratio of deity is the per se first object of faith.
Revealedness, non-appearance, and credibility are not the formal ratio of faith's object.
The articles of faith are complex secondary objects reduced to God.
Infused faith is one habit; acquired faith is many habits, one per article.
Believing what exceeds nature is reasonable by natural reason and meritorious when formed by charity.
There is no demonstration that Christ was true God or true man.
Faith and evident knowledge of God are compossible; intellect and will share the same formal object.
